text: A honeypot is really just one implementation of a much broader idea called deception technology: deliberately planting fake assets throughout an environment so that interacting with any of them is itself a reliable signal of unauthorized activity. A honeypot is a decoy system. Deception technology is the whole category.

A single honeypot only catches an attacker who happens to stumble onto that one specific system. Spreading smaller, cheaper decoys throughout the environment — on file servers, inside credential stores, inside Active Directory itself — multiplies the number of tripwires an attacker might trip, without standing up a dedicated decoy machine for each one.

A honeytoken is a fake credential, file, or database entry planted so that any access to it, or attempt to use it, triggers an alert. It isn't a system at all, just a single piece of bait sitting inside a real environment. A fake AWS access key left in a config file nobody should read is a honeytoken — the moment it's used, something is clearly wrong.

Decoy network shares apply the same idea to file systems — a fake share named something tempting, like HR-Salaries-2024, with no real data behind it and no legitimate reason for anyone to browse it. An attacker hunting for valuable targets will often enumerate shares looking for exactly this kind of name.

Fake Active Directory objects push deception into identity infrastructure itself: a decoy admin account or fake privileged group that no legitimate process ever touches, placed specifically to catch an attacker enumerating the directory to plan privilege escalation. Any interaction with it is a tripwire, because no real administrator ever has a reason to use it.

Picture a SOC planting a honeytoken credential, decoy AD accounts, and a decoy share named Backup-Credentials. An attacker who compromises a workstation through phishing reads the config file, enumerates AD groups, and browses shares — tripping all three. Any one alone would have been enough; together they confirm the compromise within minutes. Next up: why these alerts carry such an unusually low false-positive rate.
